screens.title: Securing Services with SELinux
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll learn why Mandatory Access Control, and specifically SELinux, matters for system security. Traditional file permissions protect resources based on user and group, but they can be bypassed if a privileged process is compromised. SELinux adds a second, policy-driven layer that labels files, processes, and ports with security contexts and enforces what types can interact. You will see how contexts like a process type for a web server and a content type for files guide enforcement. We will practice checking the SELinux mode with standard tools, interpreting AVC denial messages to understand why an action was blocked, and applying the right repair: temporary fixes for troubleshooting, and persistent fixes using semanage and restorecon. A common real-world scenario we will use is serving web content from a non-standard directory. You will learn how to confirm SELinux is the cause by switching to permissive mode, inspect denial messages, and then fix contexts safely so the server can read files without weakening policy. By the end you'll know how to troubleshoot denials and prefer persistent, least-privilege solutions over disabling SELinux.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Securing Services with SELinux
Securing Services with SELinux
Fundamentals of contexts, modes, and practical troubleshooting for RHEL-based systems.

This chapter teaches how SELinux labels files and processes with contexts, the meaning of types and modes, and the correct commands to diagnose and repair denials. You'll follow a hands-on scenario where a web server is blocked serving content from a non-standard directory and learn how to resolve it safely and persistently.

In this lesson
MAC vs DAC
Why labels matter even for root.
Coming up
Diagnose denials
Use journalctl, sealert, and audit2allow responsibly.
Practice
Persistent fixes
Use semanage and restorecon for permanent context changes.
Concept Map
Labels → Policy → Enforcement
Example: Web server
Process type httpd_t reads httpd_sys_content_t files. A mismatch causes AVC denials and a 403 in the browser.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you need for real-world SELinux administration. First, you will explain Mandatory Access Control and how it differs from discretionary permissions, recognizing where MAC prevents privilege escalation even for root. Second, you'll identify and describe SELinux components: contexts, types, roles, and the practical meaning of modes such as enforcing or permissive. Third, you'll learn how to check SELinux state and modes using standard commands and make temporary mode changes for troubleshooting without permanently weakening the system. Finally, you'll interpret AVC denial messages to decide whether to restore a default context, define a persistent context with semanage, or, when necessary and justified, generate a narrowly scoped policy with audit2allow. Each objective connects to hands-on commands and a principle: prefer persistent, policy-correct fixes over disabling enforcement. Understanding these objectives helps you keep systems secure while resolving real access problems.

screens.title: MAC vs DAC — Why SELinux matters
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the two models you'll compare. Discretionary Access Control grants rights based on the owner and group of a file; the owner can change permissions and grant access. Mandatory Access Control, as implemented by SELinux, ignores owner discretion for security-critical decisions and enforces a system-wide policy based on labels. This matters because a privileged process, even running as root, can be constrained by policy. A concrete example is a compromised web server: with DAC alone, the process might gain file-level permissions through the operating user. With SELinux and a correctly labeled file system, the web server process type may be allowed to read web content but explicitly prohibited from writing to system directories or executing user home files. A common misconception is that SELinux is only useful for preventing unprivileged users; in practice it limits processes and protects system integrity. The takeaway is to treat SELinux as a complementary layer: continue to manage Unix permissions, but rely on MAC to reduce blast radius if a service is exploited. Reflect: what would happen if a root-owned process is stopped by policy — would you expect standard permissions to prevent that? The answer highlights why MAC is necessary.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: DAC is owner-driven; MAC is policy-driven and enforces system-level constraints even for privileged users.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › MAC vs DAC
Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
Permissions and ownership determine access. Owners can change ACLs and file modes.
  • Simple to understand, maps to users and groups.
  • Can be overridden by root or a compromised process with elevation.
  • Insufficient for containing complex service interactions.
Analogy
DAC is like house keys: the owner can give copies freely.
Mandatory Access Control (SELinux)
System enforces a policy based on labels. Processes and files are assigned contexts that limit interactions.
  • Labels include user, role, type; type is used heavily in access rules.
  • Policy denies actions not explicitly allowed, reducing attack surface.
  • Works even when the process runs as root.
Key Takeaway
MAC reduces the blast radius of exploits by enforcing label-based policies.

screens.title: SELinux contexts and types
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux attaches a context label to files, processes, and ports. A full context contains fields such as user, role, type, and optionally sensitivity. For daily administration the most important field is the type. Types name identities like httpd_t for the web server process or httpd_sys_content_t for static web files. Policy defines what types can do: for example, the policy may allow httpd_t to read httpd_sys_content_t but deny it from writing to user_home_t. A concrete example: when you place a site in a non-standard path such as /srv/mywebapp, the directory may inherit a default or var_t type that the web server cannot read. Checking contexts with ls -Z and ps -Z lets you confirm the mismatch. A common misconception is that a simple chmod or chown will fix SELinux denials — chown affects DAC only. chcon can change a context temporarily for testing, but those changes can be overwritten by restorecon or a policy relabel. The persistent approach is semanage fcontext plus restorecon. Remember: types are the language of SELinux policy, and correcting types is the most robust way to restore service access without weakening security.

keyIdea.text: Type is the key SELinux identifier: ensure web content has httpd_sys_content_t to allow web servers read access.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › SELinux Contexts & Types
Context fields
A context commonly appears as user:role:type:level. Type is used most in access decisions.
Common types
httpd_t (process), httpd_sys_content_t (files), var_log_t (logs)
Commands to inspect:
  • ls -Z shows file contexts
  • ps -Z shows process contexts
Common mistake
Using chcon as the only fix; chcon is temporary and can be overwritten by restorecon or relabeling.
Example inspection
sudo ls -Z /srv/mywebapp
# sample output:
# drwxr-xr-x. root root unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0 index.html
If the type is default_t or var_t the policy may deny httpd_t read access. Use semanage fcontext and restorecon to map the directory to httpd_sys_content_t persistently.
Key takeaway
Correct types, not only file permissions, to restore service access securely.

screens.title: Checking SELinux status and modes
screens.narratorSegment: Before making any changes, check the system's SELinux state. The sestatus command shows whether SELinux is enabled and which mode it is running in: enforcing, permissive, or disabled. If you face a permission denial with a service, a safe diagnostic step is to temporarily switch to permissive mode with setenforce 0. This does not change the persistent configuration, it simply causes SELinux to log denials while allowing the action. After confirming that the issue disappears in permissive mode, you know SELinux enforcement is the cause, then switch back to enforcing with setenforce 1 to resume protection. Never edit /etc/selinux/config to disable SELinux for immediate troubleshooting; that requires a reboot and is a permanent policy relaxation. A typical troubleshooting flow: 1) check sestatus, 2) reproduce the problem, 3) setenforce 0 to confirm, 4) gather AVC logs with journalctl -t AVC or /var/log/audit/audit. log, and 5) apply a targeted fix. This workflow prevents unnecessary downtime and avoids the common mistake of disabling SELinux instead of diagnosing it. Checking SELinux status and modes means use setenforce to test whether selinux is the cause; then use logs to design a persistent fix rather than disabling the module.. In practical terms, use tools to confirm mode and switch safely for troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Checking Status & Modes
Common commands
sudo sestatus
# Shows SELinux status and current mode
sudo setenforce 0  # permissive
sudo setenforce 1  # enforcing
Use setenforce for immediate, temporary changes. To persist a mode across reboots edit /etc/selinux/config and reboot only when necessary.
Misconception
Switching to permissive is safe for diagnosis, but leaving it that way reduces protection. Always restore enforcing after confirming the issue.
Troubleshooting flow
  1. Check sestatus to confirm SELinux is active and mode.
  2. Reproduce the failure to capture AVC entries.
  3. Temporarily setenforce 0. If the problem clears, SELinux is implicated.
  4. Collect AVC logs: journalctl -t AVC or /var/log/audit/audit.log.
  5. Apply the least-privilege fix: restorecon, semanage fcontext, or a narrow audit2allow module.
Example
Switching to permissive allowed a web request, confirming SELinux blocked access. Logs then pointed to a wrong file context.

screens.title: Inspecting AVC denials and logs
screens.narratorSegment: When SELinux denies an operation it writes an AVC denial. These appear in the audit log or via journalctl tagged as AVC. Your job is to locate the denial that corresponds to the failed operation, identify the source process type and the target object type, and decide the correct corrective action. A typical workflow: reproduce the failure, then run journalctl -t AVC --since "5 minutes ago" or inspect /var/log/audit/audit. log. Utilities such as sealert can parse messages into human-friendly advice, but reading the raw AVC gives you the exact types and requested permissions. For example, an entry may show an httpd_t trying to write to a directory labeled var_log_t. That tells you the web server lacks write permission by policy. A common pitfall is to immediately generate an audit2allow rule; instead first consider whether restoring the default file context or adding a semanage fcontext mapping is the correct, least-privilege solution. If no suitable type exists, then generate a narrowly scoped module with audit2allow and review the generated type enforcement rules before installing them. Inspecting AVC denials and logs means match avc denial entries to the failing operation and prefer context changes over new policy when possible.. In practical terms, find the evidence selinux recorded and translate it to a fix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Inspecting AVC Denials
Collect recent AVC messages
sudo journalctl -t AVC --since "5 minutes ago"
# or
sudo cat /var/log/audit/audit.log | grep AVC
Look for the record whose timestamp matches your test. The message lists source and target types and the requested permission vector such as write or execute.
Tip
Use sealert -a to get translated advice, but verify the underlying types before changing policy.
Interpreting an example
# Simplified example line
type=AVC msg=audit(1616161616.123:456): avc:  denied  { write } for  pid=1234 comm="httpd" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t tcontext=system_u:object_r:var_log_t tclass=file
This shows httpd_t attempted to write a file labeled var_log_t and was denied. Decide: give the process a log-write type, update the file type, or generate a precise policy module if necessary.
Key takeaway
Identify source and target types in the AVC. That mapping reveals the correct, minimal action to restore functionality.

screens.title: Managing file contexts: chcon, restorecon, semanage
screens.narratorSegment: There are three tools you will use to manage file contexts. chcon changes a file's context immediately, but it is temporary and can be reset by restorecon or policy relabel. Use chcon for quick testing. restorecon consults the policy to restore default contexts; it is the tool to revert accidental changes or apply default labels after installing content. semanage fcontext lets you define a persistent mapping between a file path pattern and a context type so that future restorecon operations and relabel actions will apply your mapping. A concrete workflow: when you create /srv/mywebapp and the web server can't read it, first inspect the context with ls -Z. If the current type is incorrect, you can test chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/mywebapp to see if the server works. If that fixes the problem, create a persistent rule with sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mywebapp(/.*)?" and then run sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebapp to apply the rule. Avoid making semanage changes without testing, and prefer semanage+restorecon for long-term fixes instead of chcon alone. Managing file contexts: chcon, restorecon, semanage means use chcon to test, restorecon to apply defaults, and semanage fcontext plus restorecon to make persistent mappings.. In practical terms, when to use temporary and persistent context changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Manage File Contexts
Commands and roles
ls -Z /path            # inspect
sudo chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /path  # temporary
sudo restorecon -Rv /path  # restore defaults
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/path(/.*)?"  # persistent mapping
sudo restorecon -Rv /path  # apply mapping
Sequence: inspect → test (chcon) → persist (semanage) → apply (restorecon). This minimizes risk while ensuring durability.
Mistake to avoid
Relying solely on chcon for long-term fixes; it will not survive relabel or some package operations.
Concrete example
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mywebapp(/.*)?"
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebapp
ls -Z /srv/mywebapp  # now shows httpd_sys_content_t
After applying these commands the web server will be permitted to read the files under the newly labeled directory without additional policy changes.
Takeaway
Persistent mappings via semanage plus restorecon are best practice for production systems.

screens.title: Using audit2allow safely
screens.narratorSegment: audit2allow can convert AVC denial lines into a type enforcement file and a policy package that you can install. It can be useful when a legitimate action is blocked and no existing type or semanage mapping will address it. A common pattern is to grep relevant lines from the audit log and pipe them to audit2allow to create a module. For example, you might run grep httpd /var/log/audit/audit. log | audit2allow -M mywebserver to produce mywebserver. te and mywebserver. pp. Before installing the. pp package, open the generated. te file and inspect the rules. Verify each rule is narrowly scoped to only the required operation and does not grant broad permissions like allow all. After review, install with semodule -i mywebserver. pp. A misconception is that audit2allow is a one-click fix — in reality it automates rule generation and requires human review to avoid introducing security holes. When possible prefer restoring or mapping contexts; use audit2allow only when a new, legitimate behavior needs a custom rule and you ensure least privilege. Using audit2allow safely means use audit2allow for edge cases after reviewing generated rules; prefer context mapping for common cases.. In practical terms, generate a policy module from avc denials, but review results carefully. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete scenario you will use in the lab. You configure a web server to serve content from /srv/mywebapp and see a 403 Forbidden in the browser. First, confirm SELinux mode with sestatus. If it's enforcing, reproduce the 403 while tailing logs. Next, temporarily switch to permissive using setenforce 0 and retry the request. If the 403 disappears, SELinux denied the access. Switch back to enforcing immediately. Use journalctl -t AVC or /var/log/audit/audit. log to find the denial entry—search for your web server process name. Inspect the AVC to find the target file type. If it succeeds, make the change persistent: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mywebapp(/.*)?" followed by restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebapp. Verify with ls -Z and by accessing the page. This flow confirms SELinux involvement and uses the least-privilege persistent fix rather than disabling enforcement. screens.title: Avoiding common SELinux errors
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes administrators make with SELinux that lead to insecure or fragile systems. First, disabling SELinux permanently to solve a service issue is a blunt approach that removes an important protection layer. Instead follow the diagnose-and-fix flow. Second, relying only on chcon for persistent needs is fragile; chcon is intended for testing. Use semanage fcontext paired with restorecon for durability. Third, using audit2allow without reviewing the generated rules can open broad permissions unintentionally. Always inspect the. te file for overly permissive allow statements. Fourth, confusing DAC fixes with SELinux fixes leads to wasted effort; changing ownership or mode will not address a type mismatch. A helpful habit is to always check ls -Z and ps -Z early when investigating access failures. Lastly, remember that logs are your friend: AVC entries contain the mapping between source and target types. The corrective mindset is to answer three questions: does the action belong to the service? Is a context change appropriate? Or does a narrow policy change truly need to be created? This protects the principle of least privilege. Avoiding common SELinux errors means diagnose, test, then persist; never disable selinux as the first response and always review generated policy rules.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll learn why Mandatory Access Control, and specifically SELinux, matters for system security. Traditional file permissions protect resources based on user and group, but they can be bypassed if a privileged process is compromised. SELinux adds a second, policy-driven layer that labels files, processes, and ports with security contexts and enforces what types can interact. You will see how contexts like a process type for a web server and a content type for files guide enforcement. We will practice checking the SELinux mode with standard tools, interpreting AVC denial messages to understand why an action was blocked, and applying the right repair: temporary fixes for troubleshooting, and persistent fixes using semanage and restorecon. A common real-world scenario we will use is serving web content from a non-standard directory. You will learn how to confirm SELinux is the cause by switching to permissive mode, inspect denial messages, and then fix contexts safely so the server can read files without weakening policy. By the end you'll know how to troubleshoot denials and prefer persistent, least-privilege solutions over disabling SELinux.

These objectives map to practical skills you need for real-world SELinux administration. First, you will explain Mandatory Access Control and how it differs from discretionary permissions, recognizing where MAC prevents privilege escalation even for root. Second, you'll identify and describe SELinux components: contexts, types, roles, and the practical meaning of modes such as enforcing or permissive. Third, you'll learn how to check SELinux state and modes using standard commands and make temporary mode changes for troubleshooting without permanently weakening the system. Finally, you'll interpret AVC denial messages to decide whether to restore a default context, define a persistent context with semanage, or, when necessary and justified, generate a narrowly scoped policy with audit2allow. Each objective connects to hands-on commands and a principle: prefer persistent, policy-correct fixes over disabling enforcement. Understanding these objectives helps you keep systems secure while resolving real access problems.

These practical objectives prepare you for hands-on troubleshooting tasks. First, you will manage file and process contexts using ls -Z and ps -Z to inspect labels, and chcon for temporary changes. Second, you will learn to make persistent context mappings with semanage fcontext and apply them with restorecon so changes survive relabel operations and reboots. Third, you'll use audit2allow to generate a policy module from AVC denials when a legitimate action is blocked and no pre-existing type supports it, and you'll learn the caution needed to avoid broad rules. Fourth, you'll practice a structured troubleshooting flow: confirm SELinux mode, reproduce the denial, gather AVC logs with journalctl or audit. log, and apply the least-privilege fix. These skills will help you keep systems secure while resolving service failures without resorting to disabling SELinux.

Start by defining the two models you'll compare. Discretionary Access Control grants rights based on the owner and group of a file; the owner can change permissions and grant access. Mandatory Access Control, as implemented by SELinux, ignores owner discretion for security-critical decisions and enforces a system-wide policy based on labels. This matters because a privileged process, even running as root, can be constrained by policy. A concrete example is a compromised web server: with DAC alone, the process might gain file-level permissions through the operating user. With SELinux and a correctly labeled file system, the web server process type may be allowed to read web content but explicitly prohibited from writing to system directories or executing user home files. A common misconception is that SELinux is only useful for preventing unprivileged users; in practice it limits processes and protects system integrity. The takeaway is to treat SELinux as a complementary layer: continue to manage Unix permissions, but rely on MAC to reduce blast radius if a service is exploited. Reflect: what would happen if a root-owned process is stopped by policy — would you expect standard permissions to prevent that? The answer highlights why MAC is necessary.

SELinux attaches a context label to files, processes, and ports. A full context contains fields such as user, role, type, and optionally sensitivity. For daily administration the most important field is the type. Types name identities like httpd_t for the web server process or httpd_sys_content_t for static web files. Policy defines what types can do: for example, the policy may allow httpd_t to read httpd_sys_content_t but deny it from writing to user_home_t. A concrete example: when you place a site in a non-standard path such as /srv/mywebapp, the directory may inherit a default or var_t type that the web server cannot read. Checking contexts with ls -Z and ps -Z lets you confirm the mismatch. A common misconception is that a simple chmod or chown will fix SELinux denials — chown affects DAC only. chcon can change a context temporarily for testing, but those changes can be overwritten by restorecon or a policy relabel. The persistent approach is semanage fcontext plus restorecon. Remember: types are the language of SELinux policy, and correcting types is the most robust way to restore service access without weakening security.

Before making any changes, check the system's SELinux state. The sestatus command shows whether SELinux is enabled and which mode it is running in: enforcing, permissive, or disabled. If you face a permission denial with a service, a safe diagnostic step is to temporarily switch to permissive mode with setenforce 0. This does not change the persistent configuration, it simply causes SELinux to log denials while allowing the action. After confirming that the issue disappears in permissive mode, you know SELinux enforcement is the cause, then switch back to enforcing with setenforce 1 to resume protection. Never edit /etc/selinux/config to disable SELinux for immediate troubleshooting; that requires a reboot and is a permanent policy relaxation. A typical troubleshooting flow: 1) check sestatus, 2) reproduce the problem, 3) setenforce 0 to confirm, 4) gather AVC logs with journalctl -t AVC or /var/log/audit/audit. log, and 5) apply a targeted fix. This workflow prevents unnecessary downtime and avoids the common mistake of disabling SELinux instead of diagnosing it. Checking SELinux status and modes means use setenforce to test whether selinux is the cause; then use logs to design a persistent fix rather than disabling the module.. In practical terms, use tools to confirm mode and switch safely for troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When SELinux denies an operation it writes an AVC denial. These appear in the audit log or via journalctl tagged as AVC. Your job is to locate the denial that corresponds to the failed operation, identify the source process type and the target object type, and decide the correct corrective action. A typical workflow: reproduce the failure, then run journalctl -t AVC --since "5 minutes ago" or inspect /var/log/audit/audit. log. Utilities such as sealert can parse messages into human-friendly advice, but reading the raw AVC gives you the exact types and requested permissions. For example, an entry may show an httpd_t trying to write to a directory labeled var_log_t. That tells you the web server lacks write permission by policy. A common pitfall is to immediately generate an audit2allow rule; instead first consider whether restoring the default file context or adding a semanage fcontext mapping is the correct, least-privilege solution. If no suitable type exists, then generate a narrowly scoped module with audit2allow and review the generated type enforcement rules before installing them. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are three tools you will use to manage file contexts. chcon changes a file's context immediately, but it is temporary and can be reset by restorecon or policy relabel. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

audit2allow can convert AVC denial lines into a type enforcement file and a policy package that you can install. It can be useful when a legitimate action is blocked and no existing type or semanage mapping will address it. There are recurring mistakes administrators make with SELinux that lead to insecure or fragile systems. First, disabling SELinux permanently to solve a service issue is a blunt approach that removes an important protection layer. Instead follow the diagnose-and-fix flow. Second, relying only on chcon for persistent needs is fragile; chcon is intended for testing. Use semanage fcontext paired with restorecon for durability. Third, using audit2allow without reviewing the generated rules can open broad permissions unintentionally. Always inspect the. te file for overly permissive allow statements. Fourth, confusing DAC fixes with SELinux fixes leads to wasted effort; changing ownership or mode will not address a type mismatch. A helpful habit is to always check ls -Z and ps -Z early when investigating access failures. Lastly, remember that logs are your friend: AVC entries contain the mapping between source and target types. The corrective mindset is to answer three questions: does the action belong to the service? Is a context change appropriate? Or does a narrow policy change truly need to be created? Keep these concise ideas in mind. SELinux is a Mandatory Access Control system that enforces policies based on labels. Contexts attach metadata to files and processes; the type field is the most used in policy decisions. Modes control enforcement: enforcing blocks unauthorized actions and logs AVCs, permissive logs without blocking, and disabled turns the system off. Commands you will use daily include ls -Z and ps -Z to inspect contexts, sestatus to check mode, setenforce to switch modes temporarily, restorecon to reset defaults, semanage fcontext to create persistent mappings, and audit2allow to generate policy modules cautiously. When you face denials, prefer identifying and correcting context mismatches or creating precise semanage mappings before resorting to audit2allow. The underlying principle is least privilege: allow only the minimal access required for a service to operate.

Keep a short checklist in your mind. First: always inspect contexts with ls -Z and ps -Z when services misbehave. Second: prefer semanage fcontext plus restorecon for persistent file context changes; use chcon only for testing. Third: treat audit2allow as a last resort—generate rules only after confirming the denial is legitimate and reviewing the generated type enforcement file. These practices preserve system security while allowing necessary service behavior, and they enforce the principle of least privilege in a way that survives reboots and relabels. Ask yourself after each fix: did I allow exactly what was needed and nothing more?
